verses.text: Working together, we entreat also that you not receive the grace of God in vain,
for he says, “At an acceptable time I listened to you, in a day of salvation I helped you.”   Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation.
We give no occasion of stumbling in anything, that our service may not be blamed,
but in everything commending ourselves, as servants of God, in great endurance, in afflictions, in hardships, in distresses,
in beatings, in imprisonments, in riots, in labors, in watchings, in fastings;
in pureness, in knowledge, in perseverance, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere love,
in the word of truth, in the power of God; by the armor of righteousness on the right hand and on the left,
by glory and dishonor, by evil report and good report; as deceivers, and yet true;
as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and not killed;
as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.
Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians. Our heart is enlarged.
You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted by your own affections.
Now in return, I speak as to my children, you also be open wide.
Don’t be unequally yoked with unbelievers, for what fellowship have righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?
What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever?
What agreement has a temple of God with idols? For you are a temple of the living God. Even as God said, “I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they will be my people.”
Therefore “‘Come out from among them, and be separate,’ says the Lord. ‘Touch no unclean thing. I will receive you.
I will be to you a Father. You will be to me sons and daughters,’  says the Lord Almighty.”

footnotes.content: Paul and his team work *with* you, not at you—that's the grace here. They beg you not to let God's gift sit empty in your hands, like a feast prepared but never eaten. The work of receiving is as real as the work of giving.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah's ancient word becomes urgent now: this very hour is the acceptable time God has already chosen for you. Not tomorrow, not when you're better—*now* is when He listens, now is when He helps.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There's a tender carefulness here—Paul doesn't want anyone stumbling *because* of him, because of loose speech or hidden weakness. A servant's first work is to get out of the way, to let the gospel shine without his shadow on it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He proves his calling not by claiming perfection but by proving trustworthiness *in the middle of* affliction—beatings, hardship, despair. The Christian life isn't freedom from trouble; it's faithfulness through it. That's what commends a servant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beatings, prison, chaos, sleepless nights, hunger—Paul has walked a road most of us never imagine. Yet he doesn't boast of it; he lists it plainly, as if to say: "Look, this is real. And grace held me here too."
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What carries a servant through those trials? Not grit alone, but pureness of heart, knowledge of God, steady patience, and—this is the secret—kindness even to enemies, rooted in the Holy Spirit and real love. The inside becomes visible in the outside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Truth itself is armor—held in both hands, ready for any blow. This is not armor to attack others, but to stand unmoved: righteousness on the left hand protects the heart, righteousness on the right guards the arm that serves. God equips His messengers completely.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The world will praise you one day and revile you the next—sometimes the same people do both. Paul says: hold steady in *both*, don't let either one change who you are. Honor and shame are not your judges; Christ is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They say he's a nobody, yet the Lord knows him by name. They kill him daily, yet he lives in Christ. To outside eyes, he's defeated; to heaven's eyes, he's standing. There's a hidden life that no circumstance can touch.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sorrow and joy don't cancel each other; they teach different depths. He grieves truly over loss, yet beneath it runs an unshakeable gladness in the Lord. Empty-handed and poor, yet rich beyond measure—this paradox is the gospel lived out, not merely spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After all that suffering, Paul's heart hasn't closed—it's opened *wider*. That's courage: to let hardship enlarge your love instead of harden it. He speaks freely to Corinth because his own heart is expansive, full, ready to receive them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul isn't holding back from them—*they* are holding back from themselves. Affection is something we choose with our own will; he's saying gently, "I'm open. The door is on your side now. Don't let fear or pride lock you out of fellowship."
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He treats them as beloved children, which means he doesn't demand; he invites. "Be open wide in return"—not from obligation, but from the same generous heart he's shown them. Parents know this: sometimes the best gift is permission to trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here the tone shifts—this is not softness but clarity. Righteousness and iniquity don't make a home together; light and darkness can't share a room without one putting out the other. A believer yoked unequally will be pulled toward compromise, slowly but surely.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Christ and Belial (the adversary) have no treaty, no accord, no neutral ground. If you're bound to Christ, you can't also be bound to his opposite. That's not judgment; it's simply the nature of the thing—light doesn't negotiate with darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A temple of God cannot house idols—and *you are that temple*, dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit. This echoes Leviticus and the ancient tabernacle, but now it's you—your body, your choices. How you live declares whether God is truly welcome there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah's call—"Come out from among them"—becomes Paul's plea. Separation isn't anger; it's invitation to holiness. "Touch no unclean thing" means guard your heart carefully; God promises He will receive you, welcome you into a clean and safe space.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo of God's ancient word: He promises to be Father to those who separate themselves to Him, offering a belonging and a name that nothing else can give. As of 2026-10, His invitation remains open—not because we earned it, but because He is faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
